facts.statement: Ptyctodus lived during the late Devonian period.
The genus Ptyctodus was described by Pander in 1858.
The genus Ptyctodus includes the species P. bradyi, P. calceolus, P. compressus, P. ferox, P. molaris, and P. panderi.
facts.quote: subdivision: Ptyctodus bradyi Ptyctodus calceolus Ptyctodus compressus Ptyctodus ferox Ptyctodus molaris Ptyctodus panderi

facts.statement: Ptyctodus was an extinct fish covered in armor that lived in the late Devonian.
facts.quote: Ptyctodus is an extinct armour-plated fish of the late Devonian.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus belongs to the family Ptyctodontidae and the class Placodermi.
facts.quote: Ptyctodus belongs to the family Ptyctodontidae and is of the class Placodermi.
They share a close resemblance to modern day chimaeras (Holocephali).

facts.statement: Fossils of Ptyctodus have been found in Russia, Michigan, and Arizona, United States.
facts.quote: Fossils of this armour-plated fish have been found in locations such as in Russia, the Michigan Basis, and Arizona, United States.

facts.statement: Specimens of Ptyctodus vary in size, with measured lengths of 94, 24, and 22 millimeters.
facts.quote: Ptyctodus species come in a variety of different sizes, measured data shows three specimens being 94 millimeters, 24 millimeters, 22 millimeters in length, 23 millimeters, 6 millimeters, 4 millimeter in height, and 18 millimeters, 7 millimeters, and 4 millimeters in thickness.

facts.statement: The dental elements of Ptyctodus are very similar to those observed in chimaeroids.
facts.quote: The dentition of the Ptyctodus has dental elements that are very similarly observed in chimaeroids.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus possessed dorsal fin spines similar to those seen in Hetercanthus and Phlyctaenacanthus.
facts.quote: They were also armed with dorsal fin spines closely seen in Hetercanthus and Phlyctaenacanthus.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus exhibits sexual dimorphism in the pelvic region, with males having claspers and females having large scale-like pelvic fins.
facts.quote: Just like the other members of the family of Ptyctodontidae, there is a sexual dimorphism between the genders of Ptyctodus in the pelvic region where the characteristics are different; males had claspers, while females had large scale like pelvic fins along with their endoskeleton.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus lived as a nektonic carnivore in carbonate, lagoonal, and shallow subtidal environments.
facts.quote: Ptyctodus lived in a nektonic carnivore type-ecology and in carbonate, lagoonal, and shallow subtidal environments.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus likely fed on shellfish by crushing them with its teeth.
facts.quote: Due to structure and shape of the teeth Ptyctodus would easily be able to crush shellfish like organisms at the bottom of the ocean floors, feeding mainly off of that.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus appears to have been an agile swimmer capable of escaping predators like arthrodires.
facts.quote: They also must seem to have been very agile swimmers, able to escape predators, like arthrodires.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus bradyi was discovered in 1942 by Hussakof on Mt. Elden in Arizona based on two tooth plates.
facts.quote: Ptyctodus bradyi was discovered by the basis of two tooth plates in 1942 by Hussakof on Mt. Elden in Arizona.

facts.statement: Ptyctodus lived from the Eifelian to the Famennian stages, between 393.47 and 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Eifelian to Famennian (393.47 to 358.86 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Ptyctodus is the family Ptyctodontidae.
Ptyctodus is classified within the family Ptyctodontidae.
Ptyctodus is classified in the class Placodermi.
